paras: The Pascagoula railroad platform assault was a fight on the morning of Monday, April 4, 1881, on the railroad platform at Pascagoula, Mississippi, in which five white young men from Mobile set upon a young Black man after the two sides had cursed each other. A local magistrate broke up the fight, and no one was arrested. A Memphis roundup of regional news later reduced the episode to a report that the Mobile men had "whipped a negro."

The Pascagoula Democrat-Star reported the fight in a weekly column of "crimes and casualties," which described the past week as one "of unusual excitement" for the town. The paper believed the five young men had come from Mobile to work in the local canning factory.

Shortly before the 11:14 a.m. train arrived, the five men and a man the paper described as "a young negro, coal black" began cursing one another on the platform. After a few minutes, in the Democrat-Star's words, "they jumped the negro," and the six fought "several rounds with their fists and sticks." The Black man "stood his grounds" until Judge Randall separated the combatants. His name was not given, and no injuries were reported.
No arrests were made. The column separately noted that Ed. Blalack had "cowhided" a Black man for insulting him, without particulars.

The Democrat-Star printed the fight under the subheading "Six in a Row" and called it a "fracas," while stating that the five men began the physical attack. On April 12 the Memphis Daily Appeal's "News from Our Neighbors" column compressed the week's Pascagoula items into one paragraph, saying that "the young men from Mobile whipped a negro" and spelling the cowhider's name "Ed Bielock." The Appeal closed the paragraph with the sarcastic remark that Pascagoula was "becoming a city in a rapid manner, judging from the above indications of advanced civilization."

The Appeal's word "whipped" differs from the local account of a fight with fists and sticks in which the man fought back; the Memphis paragraph follows the local column item by item, making the Democrat-Star the better evidence.

reader.title: Pascagoula railroad platform assault
bases: Five white young men attacked one Black man with fists and sticks on a railroad platform after an exchange of curses; no organized band, warning or regulatory aim is reported, so the record's 'whitecapping' does not fit (A1, A2).
The only first-hand report is the local Democrat-Star (A1); the Memphis Appeal paragraph (A2) is a condensation of that column, not an independent account.

accounts.label: Local weekly (Pascagoula Democrat-Star)
accounts.gist: Five white young men from Mobile and a young Black man cursed each other on the platform; the five jumped him, they fought with fists and sticks, he stood his ground until Judge Randall parted them; no arrests.

accounts.label: Memphis regional roundup
accounts.gist: In one sentence of Pascagoula news, 'the young men from Mobile whipped a negro'.

framing.detail: The Democrat-Star ran it as one item in a week of local 'excitement' under the heading 'Six in a Row', describing a mutual 'fracas' while stating that the five 'jumped the negro'.
The Memphis Appeal compressed it to 'whipped a negro' and closed the Pascagoula paragraph with a sarcastic line about the town's 'advanced civilization'.

versions.value: A fist-and-stick fight in which five men jumped one man, who fought back until separated

conflicts.note: The local Democrat-Star account is the source of the Memphis paragraph and gives the detail; 'whipped' appears to be the Appeal's condensation rather than a separate report.

He stood his grounds until all bands were separated by Judge Randall. No arrests were made.
The young men are from Mobile, and we believe came out here to work in the canning factory.
